title: Gradients of Pyrophytism in Obligate Seeders: Towards a Seed Persistence Economics Spectrum
content: Persistent soil seed banks are a defining feature of many obligate-seeding species in Mediterranean-type ecosystems, yet the extent to which fire-related germination responses vary among taxa remains poorly quantified. We propose a methodological framework to detect and measure gradients of pyrophytism within obligate seeders and evaluate whether such gradients can be interpreted within a broader Seed Persistence Economics Spectrum. Using raw germination, dormancy, and viability data for ten Cistaceae species from five genera exposed to eight heat treatments (25–120 °C), we reformulate the coupled germination–viability assay as a probabilistic diagnostic test in which germination is conditional on seed viability. From contingency-table metrics, we derive ROC-point distances and F1 scores as germinability descriptors that avoid limitations associated with the biological impossibility of false-positive germination events. We then introduce the Global Minimum Dispersion of Germinability (GMDG), a variance-based metric inspired by Markowitz portfolio theory, to quantify interspecific variation in heat-triggered germination responses. Results reveal substantial heterogeneity among species traditionally classified as obligate-seeding pyrophytes. Species rankings change across the heat-treatment gradient, and several taxa exhibit responses more consistent with opportunistic exploitation of favorable post-fire conditions than with strict fire adaptation. Ordination based on GMDG identifies a continuum ranging from highly heat-responsive species to comparatively opportunistic strategists. We argue that these patterns support the existence of a Seed Persistence Economics Spectrum linking fire ecology, bet-hedging theory, life-history evolution, and plant economics frameworks through alternative evolutionary investments in establishment versus temporal seed persistence.
